notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Zechariah 2. A few things to know first:

- **Gaps:** I ran out of research tool calls before I reached the Catholic, Orthodox, modern-scholarship or Pentecostal-denomination sites (newadvent, catholic.com, oca.org, bibleodyssey, netbible, ag.org, pneumareview). So I have no notes from those sites, and none on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching.
- **Second-hand sources:** The early Church Fathers (Jerome, Cyril, Theodoret) appear here only as quoted by Barnes and Calvin. The NET Bible's view on v. 4 appears only as reported on bible.org.
- **Labels:** Tradition labels follow how the pages describe each writer.

**v. 1–2: the man with the measuring line**
- Guzik (Enduring Word, Calvary Chapel): "This was undoubtedly an angelic being and some think it was the Angel of the LORD." Jerusalem is measured to show it will be big enough for the crowds God will bring, though at the time the city had too few people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-2/
- Keil (Lutheran) also thinks the measuring man is probably the Angel of the LORD, while admitting this conjecture cannot be distinctly proved. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/2-4.htm
- The bible.org study guide says a measuring line can stand for judgment or for restoration. It also says the time in view is uncertain: Jerusalem then, the rebuilt city after the exile, or the heavenly city at the end. https://bible.org/seriespage/zechariah-2

**v. 3–4: "Run and tell that young man"**
- **Who is the young man? Most say Zechariah.** Barnes says he is the prophet himself, who was to report to his people what he heard. Pusey (Anglican, quoted by Coffman) argues "young" can't be said of angels, because they don't age. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/2-4.html
- The Pulpit Commentary agrees, but adds that the Hebrew word is used also for minister, or servant, or disciple, without necessarily defining the age. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/2-4.htm
- Calvin (Reformed) says the prophet is called a youth because he stood among angels, so the title is a humble one. https://www.ccel.org/study/Zechariah_2:4-5
- **The minority view:** The bible.org guide says the NET Bible takes the young man to be Zechariah, but disagrees. It thinks he is "the man" of v. 1, the measuring angel. https://bible.org/seriespage/zechariah-2
- **"A city without walls": the traditions really differ here.**
  - Gill (Baptist, Calvinist) says this can't mean the literal city, which got its walls under Nehemiah. It means the church of Christ in Gospel times. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/zechariah/2-4.html
  - Barnes, likewise: Clearly then it is no earthly city. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/zechariah/2-4.html
  - Guzik sees a short-term fulfillment under Ezra and Nehemiah, but clearly, its ultimate fulfillment will be rebuilding under the rule of the Messiah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-2/
  - Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel, dispensational) says the prophecy is being fulfilled today in modern Jerusalem's growth far beyond its old walls. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/2-8.html

**v. 5: wall of fire, glory within**
- Several commentators connect the wall of fire to the pillar of cloud and fire in the wilderness. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, for example, says God will be not only a defense from foes outside, but a glory within. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/2-5.htm
- Calvin: walls can be climbed, but who will dare to throw himself into the fire? https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/comment3/comm_vol30/htm/iii.iii.ii.htm
- Ellicott (Anglican) says the verse doesn't forbid building walls, which happened under Nehemiah. It is simply a solemn promise of God's protection. https://pro.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/2-5.html
- Simeon (Anglican) sees a partial fulfillment when the walls and temple were rebuilt, and the temple's greater glory when the Messiah himself came. https://pro.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/2-5.html
- Wesley (Methodist) reads "the glory" as God's presence and favour making the city glorious. Clarke (Methodist) says Much of this must refer to the New Jerusalem. https://pro.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/2-5.html ; https://studylight.org/commentaries/acc/zechariah-2.html

**v. 6–7: "Flee from the land of the north"**
- Guzik: few exiles had come back, because most were comfortable in Babylon. He reads the call to leave Babylon both literally and figuratively, linking it to Revelation 18:4–5. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-2/
- The bible.org guide:
  - "The north" means Babylon, because invaders always came into the land by the northern route.
  - The point is that God himself sent his people into exile and will bring them back.
  - "Dwell with" Babylon is a play on God's promise to dwell with his people. https://bible.org/seriespage/zechariah-2
- The Biblical Illustrator (Wardlaw) applies it to Christians today: urge God's people to leave "mystical Babylon." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/2-8.html

**v. 8: "After His Glory has sent Me…" and "the apple of His eye"**
- **Who is speaking? The Reformed and older Protestant reading says Christ.**
  - Calvin says the passage must be forcibly wrested, except it be understood of Christ: God the Father sends the Son, who is also called "the LORD." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/2-8.html
  - Barnes quotes Jerome reading it as the Saviour, sent by the Father. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/2-8.html
  - The Pulpit Commentary instead takes the speaker as the superior angel who speaks. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/2-8.htm
- **"After glory" is hard to translate.** Coffman lists several meanings scholars have proposed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/2-8.html
  - Wesley: After that he is become your glory, I am to avenge you of your enemies. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/2-8.html
  - The Pulpit Commentary: "to win honour." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/2-8.htm
  - The editor of Calvin's commentary notes that some Fathers (Eusebius, Jerome, Cyril, Theodoret) took it as the glory the Son had before he became man, a view the editor rejects. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/2-8.html
- **Whose eye?**
  - Calvin weighs both readings ("his own eye," meaning the attacker hurts himself, or God's eye) and prefers God's eye. Gill gives both. Barnes says Cyril took it as the attacker's own eye, but Jerome and Theodoret took it as God's. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/2-8.html
- **Who is the apple of God's eye today? The traditions differ.**
  - Calvin: the Church is to him like the apple of his eye. Gill: the Lord's people are members of Christ's body. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/2-8.html
  - Chuck Smith applies it directly to the Jewish people today. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/2-8.html
  - Guzik quotes Spurgeon (Baptist) on God's tender love. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-2/

**v. 9: "I will wave My hand over them"**
- Guzik: the enslavers become the enslaved, and only a shake of God's hand is needed. He says this will be ultimately fulfilled in the millennial reign of Jesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-2/
- Clarke points to Babylon's fall to the Persians. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/2-8.html
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that judgments like this are often carried out by angels in Scripture. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/2-8.htm

**v. 10: "I am coming to dwell among you"**
- Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary: Here is a prediction of the coming of Christ in human nature. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/2-13.htm
- Keil: Zion's glory commences with the coming of the Son of God in the flesh, and is completed by His return in glory. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/2-11.html
- Guzik: God's people should sing and be glad, not stay passive. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-2/

**v. 11: many nations joined to the LORD**
- **The church reading (Methodist, Baptist, Reformed):**
  - Clarke: This most certainly belongs to the Christian church.
  - Gill: the gospel preached to all nations.
  - Calvin: the nations will count themselves part of God's people.
  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/2-11.html
- Barnes calls it exactly the history of the Christian church. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/2-11.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary says single converts aren't enough: whole nations will become the Lord's people. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/2-11.html
- **The future-kingdom reading (dispensational):**
  - Constable (dispensational) puts it in the end-time day of the Lord, when the Lord returns to Jerusalem.
  - Chuck Smith reads verses 11–13 as Jesus reigning on earth for a thousand years.
  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/2-11.html
- **Sender and Sent:** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the one who sends and the one sent are both called "the LORD," so they must be One. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/2-11.htm

**v. 12: Judah his portion in "the Holy Land"**
- **The land itself:** Guzik says this is the only place in the Bible that uses the phrase "Holy Land." He argues the land itself, not just the people, is holy to God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-2/
- **Restoration of the Jews:** Clarke calls it a promise of the final restoration of the Jews. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/2-12.html
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the verse is added so the Jews won't fear losing their special place once the nations join. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Zec/Zec_002.cfm
- **A wider reading:**
  - Keil (Lutheran) says the "holy land" reaches just as far as the nations, which have become the people of Jehovah spread. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/2-13.htm
  - Barnes sees the land as a type of the worldwide church. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/2-12.html
  - The bible.org guide says the New Testament widens the Old Testament's geographical promises into a worldwide invitation. https://bible.org/seriespage/zechariah-2

**v. 13: "Be silent… all people"**
- Calvin: silence means submission. Believers keep quiet willingly, while the ungodly are silenced when God restrains them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/2-13.html
- The Pulpit Commentary: God had seemed to sleep when he let his people be trodden down, but now rises up to act. https://biblehub.com/zechariah/2-13.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the call is aimed both at proud enemy nations and at Jews who doubted God's promises. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/2-13.htm
- Gill reads the verse as being about the end times: the destruction of antichrist, the conversion of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/2-13.html
